title: Capture Recapture
summary: Estimate a hidden animal or object population using marked samples, proportional reasoning, and clear assumptions.

items.prompt: A wildlife worker marks 30 birds and releases them. Later, a sample of 20 birds contains 5 marked birds. Estimate the total bird population.
items.explanation: Use $\dfrac{30 \times 20}{5}=120$. The number marked initially is multiplied by the size of the second sample, then divided by the number of marked animals recaptured.

items.prompt: A researcher marks 80 fish. In a second catch of 45 fish, 9 are marked. Which calculation estimates the total fish population?
items.explanation: The estimate is $\dfrac{\text{number marked initially} \times \text{second sample size}}{\text{number of marked animals recaptured}}$, so the calculation is $80 \times 45 \div 9$.

items.prompt: Which assumption helps make a capture-recapture estimate reliable?

options.text: The marked animals become easier to catch than unmarked animals.
The marked animals mix evenly back into the population.
Many animals enter or leave the area between samples.
The second sample is taken from just one small part of the habitat.

items.explanation: The marked animals must mix evenly so that the second sample is representative of the whole population. Migration, biased sampling or changed catchability can make the estimate unreliable.

items.prompt: A biologist marks 55 frogs and releases them. Later, a sample of 32 frogs contains 7 marked frogs. Estimate the total population to the nearest whole frog.
items.explanation: Calculate $\dfrac{55 \times 32}{7}=251.428\ldots$. This rounds to $251$ frogs because the first digit after the decimal point is $4$.

items.prompt: A lake contains an estimated 300 fish, of which 60 have been marked. About how many marked fish would you expect in a representative second sample of 40 fish?
items.explanation: The marked proportion is $\dfrac{60}{300}=\dfrac{1}{5}$. Therefore, the expected number marked is $\dfrac{1}{5} \times 40=8$.
